title: The Trump administration halted a Great Lakes project. Then Whitmer called Trump
description: An unexplained Trump administration hold on construction of a state-federal project aimed at preventing invasive carp from reaching the Great Lakes was abruptly lifted this week, hours after a call to...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — An unexplained Trump administration hold on construction of a state-federal project aimed at preventing invasive carp from reaching the Great Lakes was abruptly lifted this week, hours after a call to President Donald Trump by Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

The Army Corps had halted work without explanation on the Brandon Road Interbasin Project near Joliet, Illinois, in July, leaving officials in Illinois and Michigan struggling for answers about the pause even as environmental officials warned that invasive carp were being found alarmingly close to Lake Michigan.

Then Whitmer, a Democrat, called Trump.

The Wednesday phone call was a surprising intervention by the Democratic governor, who has developed an unusual relationship with a president who was once one of her fiercest political foes. Hours after the call, the stop-work order was lifted.

The episode underscores not only the unusual cross-party relationship Whitmer has cultivated with Trump, but also the top-down and relationship-driven nature of his administration — where direct phone calls and displays of deference to the president remain the best way to get things done.

"Governor Whitmer spoke with President Trump today to ask him to direct the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to lift the stop-work order," Bobby Leddy, a spokesperson for Whitmer, said in a statement. "The governor underscored the urgency of the moment, noting that invasive carp were recently found just 80 miles from Lake Michigan — farther up the Illinois River than ever recorded."

Whitmer's office said that Wednesday they had been notified that work on the project could resume. The White House referred questions to the Army Corps of Engineers, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Illinois, Michigan and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers have spent years planning a gantlet of technologies in the Des Plaines River near Joliet to keep invasive carp from reaching Lake Michigan. The project has repeatedly faced uncertainty under Trump, despite his public support for it and hundreds of millions of dollars in federal funding approved under President Joe Biden.

In March, Whitmer pressed Trump to release federal funding for Brandon Road. Trump soon posted on Truth Social that he was "working with Governor Gretchen Whitmer" to protect the Great Lakes from invasive carp, and the Army Corps released funding for the project's next phase the following month. The administration then issued another stop-work order in July, saying the project was undergoing an administrative review but offering little explanation.

"It's time for the Trump Administration to uphold the federal government's obligations, stop playing political games, and move this project forward," Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said in a July 30 statement.

The urgency increased in August, when the Illinois Department of Natural Resources detected hundreds of juvenile invasive carp about 80 miles from Lake Michigan, the first time carp of that size had been found that far upstream since monitoring began in 2010.

Whitmer, who is term-limited and set to leave office in January, has operated more freely with Trump during his second term after the two sparred repeatedly during his first. She has traveled to the White House to meet with him and welcomed him to Michigan, drawing criticism at times from fellow Democrats for her willingness to work with the Republican president.

Yet even after Michigan officials received word that the stop-work order had been lifted, officials in Illinois — where the project is located — had not been notified of the decision, raising questions about whether the project could remain in flux.

In stark contrast to Whitmer, Pritzker has emerged as one of Trump's most outspoken critics among the nation's governors as he considers mounting a bid for the 2028 Democratic nomination to replace him.

"Despite the Brandon Road Interbasin Project being in Illinois, the state has received no new communication from the Trump administration," Matt Hill, spokesperson for Pritzker, wrote in a statement. "You would expect if the administration really cared about protecting the Great Lakes they would notify Illinois."

title: Spain's leader struggles to answer lawmakers about Ceuta border crisis
description: A day after tens of thousands of Spaniards protested the government’s handling of the Ceuta border crisis, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez struggled to field lawmakers' questions about the matter, includ...
fullText:
MADRID (AP) — A day after tens of thousands of Spaniards protested the government's handling of the Ceuta border crisis, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez struggled to field lawmakers' questions about the matter, including what role Morocco played in the deadly mass crossing in July.

Five weeks after the incident, few answers have been provided about how 72,000 people were able to stream across the border shared by the Spanish exclave in North Africa and Morocco. While rejecting suggestions that Moroccan authorities helped orchestrate the incident, Sánchez said Moroccan police "allowed the border to be crossed."

He said his government would release key reports about the border breach soon, but did not say when they would be made public or what they would entail.

In his remarks, the Spanish leader said 141 people had died during the mass crossing, up from the most-recent official estimate of 96 deaths in Spain and Morocco, provided by authorities in Ceuta and Morocco's National Human Rights Council. Neither his office nor the interior ministry could say how it had been tallied when contacted by The Associated Press.

Sánchez is facing mounting scrutiny amid a prolonged humanitarian crisis in Ceuta, where the flood of thousands of migrants has angered residents in the tiny community, which is ill-equipped to handle such an influx.

In the event's aftermath, top officials in the Sánchez government have at times provided conflicting information. Last week, Spain's Defense Minister Margarita Robles said Spanish intelligence had provided prior warning of the border rush, while Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said it had not.

Spaniards on Wednesday joined protests in support of Ceuta, demanding solutions to the city's ongoing tensions and calling for Sánchez to step down. The crisis is shaping up to be one of the most serious threats his government has faced. Sánchez faced a barrage of questions on Thursday from lawmakers after his opening address alongside calls for early elections.

"The people of Ceuta have been without normalcy, without security and without answers for over a month. And we Spaniards are at the same time perplexed and outraged in the face of the violation of our territorial integrity," said opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the center-right Popular Party.

"Why are you afraid of Morocco?" Feijóo asked.

Most of the migrants who crossed into Ceuta in late July returned within days to neighboring Morocco or were ushered back. But around 5,000 people, including 1,200 minors, remain in the city weeks later, according to the national government. Ceuta's local government cites a higher figure of about 9,000 people.

Sánchez, who faces an election next year, has said a misinterpretation of a Supreme Court ruling and disinformation on social media encouraged people to rush the border.

The prime minister has also accused social media accounts linked to Russia and Israel and right-wing groups of exploiting and amplifying the Ceuta crisis after it happened on July 30 and 31. Israel and Russia have denied the claim.

Sánchez also maintained there was no evidence Morocco's government was behind the mass crossing.

"I can assure you that no institution — neither the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, nor any international body — has provided the Spanish government with solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None," Sánchez said.

Earlier this week, Spanish media reported that a police report had highlighted the alleged permissiveness of Moroccan security forces in the incident, but Spanish officials denied that the document blamed the Moroccan government.

Sánchez acknowledged that for a 10-hour period on July 30 when migrant arrivals peaked, Morocco's Gendarmerie police "allowed the border to be crossed" in Ceuta, but said the same force effectively took control of it later.

As questions have grown on the right and left in Spain about Morocco's role in the border rush, the Spanish leader said he would only take action if he had evidence about Rabat's involvement.

"For the record, if such solid evidence existed, we would act accordingly with absolute decisiveness, as the situation demands," he said.

Sánchez condemned comments from two Moroccan ministers questioning the sovereignty of Ceuta and Melilla, Spain's other territory in North Africa. Morocco's ambassador in Madrid had been summoned by Spain over the remarks, he said.

Morocco's Foreign Ministry did not respond to questions from the AP seeking comment about the diplomatic row or the Spanish police report.

The two exclaves have the European Union's only land borders with Africa.

Akram Oubachir in Casablanca, Morocco, and Renata Brito in Barcelona contributed to the report.

title: Marijuana users may face hidden driving danger that standard tests can miss
description: Cannabis edible users registered THC levels nearly 10 times lower than smokers despite similar driving impairment, exposing a potential road safety gap.
fullText:
A new study warns that driving after eating cannabis edibles can significantly impair road performance and reaction times, even if blood tests show THC levels far below the legal limit.

The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, highlight a potential challenge for impaired-driving enforcement in Canada and some U.S. jurisdictions.

Most previous cannabis-driving studies have involved smoked or inhaled marijuana, which more rapidly spikes levels of THC (tetrahydrocannabinol, the main psychoactive compound in cannabis) in the bloodstream.

America Hits Major Marijuana Milestone As Daily Weed Use Surpasses Daily Drinking

Edibles are absorbed more slowly and can produce driving impairment even when blood THC concentrations remain relatively low.

Researchers found that drivers who consumed higher doses of edible THC struggled with lane control, had slower reaction times and experienced greater speed fluctuations. Yet, their blood tests stayed below the standard legal cutoff used to prove impairment at roadside traffic stops.

To assess how oral cannabis impacts driving, researchers at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto conducted a trial with 40 healthy adult volunteers who regularly use cannabis.

Each participant attended four separate sessions in which they consumed soft-chew gummies containing either 0, 2, 10 or 20 milligrams of THC.

Cannabis Compounds Could Reverse Disease Affecting One-third Of Adults

The researchers then tested the drivers using a driving simulator at two, five and 24 hours after consumption, tracking how well drivers stayed in their lane, how quickly they reacted to road events and how consistently they maintained their speed.

Blood samples and self-reported ratings of intoxication were also collected.

The results showed driving impairment at two and five hours after consuming 10- and 20-milligram gummies. Compared with placebo, participants who consumed those doses had greater variability in lane position, while the 20-milligram dose was also linked to slower reaction times and less consistent speed control.

Participants also recognized their own limitations, reporting a lower willingness to drive and reduced confidence in their driving skills after taking the gummies.

The highest blood THC concentrations averaged 1.6 nanograms per milliliter after the 10-milligram dose and 3.4 nanograms per milliliter after the 20-milligram dose. Those levels were below the commonly used 5-ng/mL threshold, although THC limits vary by jurisdiction and some individual samples exceeded 5 ng/mL.

The study did have some limitations. Tests were conducted on virtual simulators rather than actual roads, meaning drivers faced no real physical risk during the experiments. It also focused on regular cannabis users, so it is unclear how occasional users might react to similar doses.

Additionally, minimal residual effects were detected after 24 hours. While maximum speed remained slightly higher among participants on the 10-milligram and 20-milligram doses, subjective feelings of intoxication had completely faded.

In an accompanying commentary, Dr. José Ignacio Nazif-Munoz of the Université de Sherbrooke noted that these biological differences pose a challenge for law enforcement.

Because edibles are absorbed slowly through the digestive system, standard blood tests may fail to identify unsafe drivers, leaving policymakers searching for more reliable roadside tools.

"The delayed absorption and prolonged duration of effects of edible cannabis distinguish it from smoked or inhaled cannabis, complicating the interpretation of biological measures," he wrote.

title: Military personnel told last month to stop calling Iran conflict "Operation Epic Fury"
description: The Pentagon says "Operation Epic Fury" ended on May 5, after an Air Force email last month told service members to stop using the name for ongoing Iran operations.
fullText:
Washington — An Air Force email from August, obtained by CBS News, shows the Pentagon was instructing personnel to stop referring to the ongoing U.S. military operations in Iran as "Operation Epic Fury" — three months after the Trump administration declared it had ended.

In response to questions from CBS News, the Pentagon said Wednesday that Operation Epic Fury officially ended May 5, the same day Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared to reporters at the White House: "The operation is over. Epic Fury is — the president notified Congress — we're done with that stage of it. We're now on to this Project Freedom." Four days earlier, Mr. Trump told Congress the "hostilities" had "terminated."

Previously, the Pentagon and U.S. Central Command had declined to disclose the operation's formal end date for months. The U.S. and Iran have continued to exchange on-and-off fire since Operation Epic Fury's official end date, though there have been lengthy pauses in fighting, including during a ceasefire that began in early April.

But the date also raises questions about how the Pentagon categorizes service members who were killed and wounded after "Operation Epic Fury" formally ended, or why guidance over what to call ongoing U.S. military operations against Iran came months after the May end date.

Last month, as senior U.S. Air Force leaders flew to Orlando, Florida, to attend the 2026 Air Force Sergeants Association, high-level public affairs officers were instructed to inform military leaders not to use "Operation Epic Fury." They were told to instead use broader language to refer to the conflict: "overseas operations in the [U.S. Central Command Area of Responsibility]," according to an email containing the guidance that was obtained by CBS News and dated Aug. 7.

The Air Force email shows that the guidance was issued by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's central public affairs office led by Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesman. It reiterated that U.S. Central Command had to approve information publicly released about the Iran conflict.

U.S. military officials who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity said the guidance was not exclusive to the U.S. Air Force and was disseminated across the entire Defense Department. Military officials, who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said the guidance was also disseminated within their services in August and September.

Contacted by CBS News, a Defense Department official said: "Following the April ceasefire, the administration stated Operation Epic Fury had concluded on May 5. Subsequent activities have included Freedom of Navigation operations and strikes to further diminish threats posed by the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] to commercial shipping, Gulf countries, and American forces."

The U.S. military has historically published start and end dates for named military operations, creating a public record of when one mission ends and another begins. Operation Enduring Freedom in Afghanistan, for example, began Oct. 7, 2001, and ended on Dec. 31, 2014, before moving into Operation Freedom's Sentinel

The Pentagon used those dates to establish campaign phases and eligibility for military awards, but they also provide Congress, service members and the public with a clear way to track the scope and duration of American military involvement in operations abroad.

Rubio appears to be the only Trump administration official to publicly and explicitly say that Operation Epic Fury had officially concluded. He did not, however, say that the date it ended was May 5.

On the same day as Rubio's statement, Hegseth also separately briefed reporters at the Pentagon, differentiating Epic Fury from the new Project Freedom, which he described as a defensive maritime mission to protect commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. He referred to Epic Fury in the past tense but did not explicitly state that the operation had ended. In a Pentagon press briefing a month earlier in April, after the U.S. and Iran entered into a temporary ceasefire, Hegseth said Epic Fury had achieved a "decisive military victory."

May 5 was also the last time the Pentagon briefed the press on the war with Iran. Mr. Trump announced on May 5 that Project Freedom would be put on hold for a "short period of time" so the U.S. and Iran could negotiate. Its current status is not clear.

The May 5 date did not mark the end of the broader conflict with Iran. American forces continue to conduct missions tied to the conflict that began six months ago when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.

President Trump formally notified Congress that "military action" against Iran had restarted on July 7, in a message addressed to Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, the Senate's president pro tempore. At around that time, talks between the U.S. and Iran collapsed, and Mr. Trump declared the April ceasefire "over."

Iranian forces have continued attacks on U.S. troops and commercial vessels following the collapse of the April ceasefire. The U.S. has also periodically struck Iran, including in two different rounds of strikes this week that drew Iranian counterattacks.

The Pentagon's acknowledgment of the May 5 date raises questions about why its public affairs office found it necessary in early August to explicitly instruct senior leaders not to use the Operation Epic Fury banner when talking about ongoing military operations against Iran, an operation the military now says had ended months earlier. The Pentagon did not comment on why the guidance was sent out.

Separately, the significance of the May 5 date also extends beyond the named operation, providing a benchmark for understanding how the military has counted the Americans killed and wounded in the fighting since the war with Iran started.

In July, the Defense Department website that informs the public about the dead and wounded in military conflicts originally categorized four service members who died in July in the Mideast as being killed in action during Operation Epic Fury — two months after it had officially ended.

On July 18, 1st Lt. Tyler James Feehan, Staff Sgt. Angel Rampersad and Pfc. Isabella Gonzales were killed when an Iranian missile hit their sleeping barracks at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan. The fourth service member, Staff Sgt. Michael Emmanuel Swinton, was killed in a separate incident on July 19, in Iraq, during a controlled detonation of an Iranian attack drone.

Within a few days, the four were moved on the Defense Department's website into a new category, "overseas operations," which was created over the weekend of July 25. The move technically decreased the number killed in Epic Fury hostilities from 18 to 14.

When the four deceased service members were moved to the overseas operations category, multiple news outlets, including CBS News, requested to know why. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell on July 23 chalked up the errors to a "temporary data disruption" and said the "site anomalies" were being resolved. The Pentagon also declined to say in July when Epic Fury had ended.

Contacted for this story, a Pentagon official said: "Since Operation Epic Fury has concluded, the Department classifies casualties as overseas operations in the CENTCOM area of responsibility."

As of publication, the Pentagon's Defense Casualty Analysis System currently shows five service members were wounded in June, and one was killed in July in Operation Epic Fury. It's not clear why these service members are categorized under the operation that the Pentagon says ended in May or why no end date for Epic Fury is listed.

title: Young Orthodox Christians take part in a lights procession in Romania’s capital
description: Thousands of young Orthodox Christians gathered in Romania’s capital for a candlelit procession that illuminated a trail from the giant National Cathedral to Patriarchate Hill, a historic site conside...
fullText:
BUCHAREST, Romania (AP) — Thousands of young Orthodox Christians gathered in Romania's capital for a candlelit procession that illuminated a trail from the giant National Cathedral to Patriarchate Hill, a historic site considered sacred to Romanian Orthodoxy.

The Procession of Lights was part of a four-day program for the eighth edition of the International Meeting of Orthodox Youth in Bucharest. The annual gathering brings together 2,400 people aged 16 to 35, many from Romania and its diaspora and other Orthodox churches.

Pilgrims from dozens of countries carried candles and flags through Bucharest's streets as they made their way to Patriarchate Hill, home to the headquarters of the Romanian Patriarchate, and the Patriarchal Residence and Cathedral.

Romania is one of the most pious countries in the European Union, with around 85% of the population identifying as religious. The Romanian Orthodox Church is a powerful institution that plays a central role in many people's lives.

In his opening speech Tuesday, Patriarch Daniel said the gathering provides "a concrete opportunity to intensify the mission of young people in the life of the Church today" in what he described as a "rapidly secularizing society."

"The young Orthodox Christian is a blessing to his family, a model for other young people and a missionary in the life of the Church," he said. "Being young in the Church means above all having the desire and courage to testify to eternal Christian values ​​in a world fascinated by ephemeral models and values."

The theme of this year's edition, "Young people, Family and Life in Christ," is relevant because "today's young generation faces specific challenges," some of which the organizers described on their website as technological hyperconnectivity, loneliness, a lack of role models and the search for the meaning of life.

"The church is a young people's place where they can find refuge and solace," Paula Pantea, a 24-year-old attendee, told The Associated Press. "They can find … friends that came to share the same thought: the young people are not alone in the Church, and the Church is here for them."

The Procession of Lights on Wednesday began at the People's Salvation Cathedral, known as the National Cathedral, which is the world's largest Christian Orthodox church. The cathedral opened last year after 15 years of construction and has an inner capacity for 5,000 worshippers. The Romanian Orthodox Church has called the cathedral "a symbol of national identity."

Adrian Agachi, a priest and press office coordinator for the Romanian Patriarchy, said that attendees — who he said came from 40 countries — will join Orthodox believers from all over Romania on Thursday for a holy liturgy at the National Cathedral.

McGrath reported from Leamington Spa, England.

title: FACT FOCUS: Trump claims US banks cannot operate in Canada. That's not true
description: Asked about the trade war with Canada on Wednesday, President Donald Trump falsely claimed that U.S. banks are not allowed to do business with its neighbor to the north.  The allegation came during a ...
fullText:
Asked about the trade war with Canada on Wednesday, President Donald Trump falsely claimed that U.S. banks are not allowed to do business with its neighbor to the north.

The allegation came during a meeting with U.S. travel executives in the Oval Office, after a reporter asked Trump whether there are plans for renewed trade talks between the two countries.

Experts say that although they may face restrictions, U.S. banks are not forbidden from operating in Canada.

Here's a closer look at the facts.

TRUMP: "They have their banks here, Bank of Canada, all of their big banks — big, beautiful banks. I think they have six or seven major banks here. We don't have our banks there. You know why? They don't allow it."

THE FACTS: There are currently 15 U.S.-based banks operating out of Canada, either as branches or subsidiaries, according to a spokesperson for the Canadian Bankers Association. Certain restrictions can make it difficult for U.S. banks to compete north of the border, experts say, but they are free to enter the market. There are eight Canadian banks operating in the U.S., according to the Federal Reserve's most recent data. The Bank of Canada is not one of them — it is Canada's central bank, equivalent to the Federal Reserve in the U.S., not a commercial enterprise.

"I think some confusion arises from the differences between the U.S. and Canadian regulatory systems," said James Thompson, a professor of finance at the University of Waterloo in Canada's Ontario province. "U.S. banks are certainly permitted to operate in Canada, but how they choose to enter the Canadian market affects what they can do."

There are three categories of banks in Canada — Schedule I, Schedule II and Schedule III. Canadian-owned banks are Schedule I. There are six major Schedule I banks whose combined assets eclipse those of the 28 smaller banks in the country.

Foreign entities can choose to operate as either Schedule II or Schedule III banks. Schedule II banks are foreign-owned subsidiaries incorporated in Canada that fall under essentially the same banking framework as banks owned domestically. Schedule III banks are branches of foreign banks that are not incorporated in Canada and therefore face regulatory restrictions such as high deposit minimums. Most U.S.-owned banks operate in Canada as Schedule III institutions.

Nathalie Bergeron, a spokesperson for the Canadian Bankers Association, said that U.S.-based bank branches and subsidiaries operating in Canada have combined assets of approximately $124.6 billion in Canadian dollars (US$904 million) — more than half of all assets held by foreign bank subsidiaries and branches.

"These banks specialize in a range of financial services, including corporate and commercial lending, treasury services, credit card products, investment banking and mortgage financing," she said. "They serve not only customers with cross-border business activities, but also Canada's domestic retail market."

Among the U.S. banks doing business in Canada are J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, Citibank, Bank of America, Capital One, and Wells Fargo.

Both Schedule II and Schedule III banks face restrictions due to Canadian banking regulations. Jeremy Kronick, a financial and monetary policy expert who is president and CEO of the Canadian C.D. Howe Institute think tank, explained that Schedule III banks cannot accept deposits below $150,000 (US$72,529). This means most people won't be able to use them as their retail bank. He added that since Schedule II banks are separate legal entities from their foreign parent company, they need their own local capital and liquidity structures — an inefficient option from the bank's perspective.

Such restrictions may be the reason the majority of U.S.-owned banks choose not to do business over the border. There are more than 3,700 domestically-owned commercial banks in the U.S., according to the Federal Reserve, compared to the 15 with a presence in Canada.

"Canada is a relatively small market, and incumbent Canadian banks are already very large institutions with established brands, extensive branch networks and longstanding customer relationships," said Thompson. "For a U.S. bank contemplating entry, building the infrastructure necessary to compete for Canadian retail customers would be expensive, while initially capturing only a small share of an already relatively small market."

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Woman who fatally shot man during confrontation over parking space won't be charged
description: Prosecutors found she had a right to stand her ground, under Florida law.
fullText:
A Florida woman who fatally shot a man in the parking lot of a Walmart during a confrontation over a parking space won't face charges, prosecutors announced Thursday.

The Broward County State Attorney's Office said Florida's "stand your ground" law makes the shooter, who said she was acting in self-defense, immune from prosecution in connection with the June 30 shooting in North Lauderdale.

Bart Diguglielmo, 62, was shot and killed in the incident, which was captured on several videos, including from cellphones and a Tesla, according to a memo on the shooting released Thursday by the Broward County State Attorney's Office.

Man fatally shot in Walmart parking lot following dispute over parking space: Authorities

"A dispute over a parking space. In a Walmart parking lot. The facts surrounding the June 30, 2026, homicide of Bart DiGuglielmo are as tragic as they are absurd," Broward State Attorney's Office Homicide Trial Unit Division Chief Stephen Zaccor wrote in the memo. "There is relatively no dispute about what actually happened because the entire incident was captured by various video recording devices."

The shooter, identified in the memo as Melissa Payne, was driving with her niece and niece's baby when she and Diguglielmo got into a "brief stalemate" after attempting to park in the same spot, the memo said.

DiGuglielmo "inexplicably abandoned his car in the through lane of travel" and went into the store, before shortly returning to his vehicle, according to the memo. Multiple witnesses reported hearing him say he was going to "mess her car up" and "---- her s--- up," before driving off at a high rate of speed, parking and then walking toward Payne's vehicle, according to the memo. A witness described him as being "visibly angry" while looking at Payne, according to the memo.

Payne exited her vehicle holding a phone in her left hand and a firearm in her right and said, per a witness, "If you keep coming up to me, I'm going to ------- shoot you!" the memo stated.

The witness reported that "despite those warnings," DiGuglielmo continued to approach, and video showed him "aggressively approach" Payne, according to the memo.

DiGuglielmo "continued his pursuit" as Payne backed away from him, according to the memo. He is seen on video continuing to pursue her and "motioned as if he was going to damage" her vehicle with his keys, according to the memo.

DiGuglielmo turned back and then approached Payne, at which point she fired her gun, striking him in the abdomen, according to the memo.

Payne was on the phone with her husband during the shooting, who told authorities that she said, "Bae, I shot. Call the cops," according to the memo.

She was briefly taken into custody by the Broward Sheriff's Office and her "recitation of the facts was consistent with the various sources of video evidence," the memo stated. She was released after stating she acted in self-defense, prosecutors said.

2 killed, multiple hurt in shooting at Minneapolis apartment building: Police

In an analysis of the incident, Zaccor stated that Payne was "in a public place, a Walmart parking lot, and therefore was in a place she had a right to be." She further is not a convicted felon and had a right to possess a firearm, "therefore she was not doing anything unlawful at the time she used deadly force," he wrote.

"Accordingly," Zaccor continued, Payne "had the right to stand her ground if she was in reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm." Based on the evidence, the state is unable to prove that her fear of great bodily harm was "not reasonable," he wrote, citing DiGuglielmo's actions.

Zaccor said that because Florida is a stand-your-ground state, Payne "did not have to wait to be attacked before resorting to deadly force. She did not have to retreat as long as her fear was reasonable and no evidence has been presented to disprove that."

title: US probes Iran wedding strike that analysis shows was likely direct hit by US munition
description: , Edward Carron, Idrees Ali and George Sargent Sept 4 (Reuters) - U.S.
fullText:
Sept 4 (Reuters) - U.S. Vice President JD Vance said that the United States was investigating a deadly strike on an Iranian wedding earlier this week that an analysis published by Reuters showed likely resulted from a direct hit by a U.S. munition.

An explosion ‌that ripped through a wedding celebration in southern Iran on Tuesday likely resulted from a direct hit by a U.S. munition and not a ricochet off another ‌target, according to an analysis on Thursday by weapons experts who reviewed images and video verified by Reuters.

The United States has not accepted responsibility for the incident. President Donald Trump's administration is facing growing domestic public pressure to ​end a war that is weighing on his approval ratings ahead of crucial November midterm elections.

Iranian state television on Thursday said that a 22-year-old woman had died in hospital following the strike that hit a home during a wedding, taking the total reported death toll to five. Iranian officials said that nearly 70 were wounded.

Funeral-goers assembled in the late afternoon on Thursday outside the village of Kuhestak in Sirik County, along a stretch of the Strait of Hormuz coast that was hit by heavy U.S. airstrikes late on Tuesday to mourn their loved ones.

Vance told reporters on Thursday ‌that the United States was looking into the incident. "We're investigating it ⁠because obviously we care. We want to know," he said.

"If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran, when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them," Vance added.

The U.S. military said it was aware ⁠of the Iranian reports but it "never targets civilians".

A U.S. official speaking on condition of anonymity said the government is looking at various scenarios related to the casualties at the wedding, including whether they were caused by a U.S. strike, some sort of ricochet of an Iranian air defence missile, or an errant interceptor itself.

Three of the experts said the munition was likely a ‌U.S. weapon, rather than an errant Iranian air defence missile. One of the experts said the weapon may have simply missed its objective.

The incident came some six months after a missile destroyed a primary school in an incident that Iranian officials said killed more than 175 children and teachers.

At the funeral on Thursday for four victims from the wedding, Iran's Mehr news agency video showed a pickup truck carrying a flag-draped coffin beneath a canopy of palm fronds.

A reporter in front of the truck said, "This is the body of Martyr Amir-Mohammad Karimi, a 4-year-old ‌child who was martyred in an attack on the country's south by the criminal American regime."

In other ​footage of the funeral, mourners threw petals into the air as doleful music played from a loudspeaker. A casket ​was carried past a row of soldiers standing at attention with rifles.

"If it ​was a military location, it wouldn't be so painful. This was a wedding ceremony, but they turned people's joy into mourning," the semi-official Tasnim news ‌agency quoted a local man as saying.

Washington launched the airstrikes on Tuesday, ​hitting what it said were military targets along ​the coast in retaliation for Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

The sudden escalation of the Iran war has caused a surge in oil prices to levels unseen since July. Prices rose for a fourth straight day on Thursday, taking Brent crude futures over $96 a barrel. [O/R]

Iran reported 18 dead in the last U.S. assault.

It ​responded on Wednesday to the U.S. strikes with attacks on U.S. ‌bases in Iraq, Jordan, Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain, and carried out further attacks early on Thursday, saying it was targeting another U.S. base, in Kuwait.

Kuwait's military ​said its air defences had intercepted missiles and drones.

But following that, the war's biggest flare-up since July appeared to subside, with no more major attacks from ​either side reported on Thursday.

title: The Best Fitness Trackers to Give As Gifts
description: Including my favorite budget and high-end picks.
fullText:
This year was an interesting one for smart rings and smart bands, and we ended up with a few new devices that mark serious improvements on what was available before. With these new developments in mind, here are my picks for the best fitness trackers to consider giving (or asking for) as gifts this year.

I’ll have recommendations below for athletes, runners, and people with higher budgets, but before we get into those, let me present the best fitness tracker for most people: the Fitbit Air.

Google now owns the Fitbit brand, and it spent the past few years making questionable choices about its software and mostly neglecting the brand’s iconic hardware. Then, in a stunning turnaround, Google launched the smallest, lightest, and most comfortable fitness tracker I’ve ever used (not counting rings, but we’ll get to those).

The Fitbit Air tracks your steps, sleep, and workouts without needing much attention from you. Its battery lasts a week, its app reports all the standard information without a subscription, and the price is sensible for such minimalist hardware: $99.99. The only real downside is the overly chatty AI built into the app, which you can disable if it annoys you as much as it did me.

If you have $499 to spare (or $399 for some colors), the tracker to get is the Oura Ring 5. Smart rings have always been pretty clunky, but for the fifth generation, Oura managed to get its ring to a size that blends in with jewelry rings. I’ve been wearing Oura rings since the gen 2, and this is the first one that really feels like you can forget you’re wearing a device.

You pay for the privilege, of course: The purchase price, plus a $5.99/month subscription fee. But Oura’s app is one of the nicest and easiest to use of any smart ring I’ve tried. Besides just giving you daily sleep scores, it breaks down your data to show things like how well you’re recovering despite stress, and how regular your bedtimes are.

Smart rings aren’t great for detailed workout tracking (or for strength training), but they’re excellent for casually monitoring how much exercise you end up getting throughout your day. For somebody who either doesn’t need workout tracking, or tracks their workouts with another device, an Oura is great for the rest of their day.

Some people may want more information than what the Fitbit Air or Oura Ring can give. If they still want to avoid having a screen on their wrist all day, the perfect pick for this person is a Whoop 5.0, specifically with the Peak (middle tier) subscription.

To explain the pricing: You’ll pay $239 for a Whoop band bundled with your first year’s subscription. After that expires, if you want to keep using it, you need to pay another $239 (or $199, if you want to downgrade your subscription and lose some of the features). That makes it more expensive than my top pick, the Fitbit Air.

But for an athlete who wants data to pore over, the Whoop seriously delivers. During workouts, you can see your heart rate zones on your phone’s screen, which the Fitbit doesn’t offer. The app can also guide you through weekly plans that are specific to your goals—say, totaling a certain number of minutes of zone 4 and 5 training, while also keeping a consistent bedtime and avoiding screens at night. The app is great at analyzing how the habits you log affect your sleep and recovery, and it’s easy to customize toward the goals you actually care about. I find it easy to balance perfectly so you don’t get information overload.

The only real downside is that many athletes may want something that gives them pace or heart rate data on their wrist. If your recipient already has a fitness watch, they can use it for workouts while using the Whoop for the rest of the day, and Whoop will seamlessly pull in workout data from the other device. That said, read on if you’re looking for an actual fitness watch with a display.

You probably thought I was going to recommend a Garmin—and I will, below—but first let me tell you why the Coros Pace 4 is a hidden gem, my personal favorite, and my best overall pick for most runners.

First, the price. It’s $249, which is cheap in the running-watch world. But it punches way above its weight, with dual-band GPS for accurate pace and distance tracking, a heart rate sensor that performed well in my extensive testing, and a fun and useful extra in its voice training logs.

You’d have to pay twice as much for a Garmin with all of those features—specifically, the Forerunner 570. Buying a nice Coros (or a Suunto, for that matter) feels like you’re getting away with something.

If there’s a runner in your life you love very much (and want your budget to reflect that), you can’t beat the Forerunner 970. Our resident marathoner Meredith Dietz has an in-depth review here that you might like to check out, but as a spoiler: She loved it.

The Forerunner 970 packs in all the features a running watch could possibly have. It’s got all the core features of more basic watches like the Coros I mentioned above, plus onboard maps, so you can see where you are in the world by glancing at your wrist.

The 970 also has a ton of performance metrics and tools to plan your training, plus a feature everyone loves: an LED flashlight that can shine on what’s in front of you without interfering with your view of the watch. If you’re looking for the best fitness watch out there, I can’t think of one that’s better than the 970.

title: Donovan won't 'underestimate' fired-up McKenna
description: Paddy Donovan insists he is not "underestimating" Tyrone McKenna before they meet at Croke Park on Saturday with a second crack at world honours on the horizon.
fullText:
Paddy Donovan insists he is not "underestimating" Tyrone McKenna before they meet at Croke Park on Saturday with a second crack at world honours on the horizon.

Donovan bounced back from his first title defeat by Lewis Crocker with an impressive victory over Karen Chukhadzhian in May to return to the mandatory slot for the IBF welterweight title held by Australia's Liam Paro.

The Limerick man is aware of the risks in taking a fight in the interim, but felt this was too good an opportunity to turn down and plans to put on a show to elevate his status.

He and McKenna have sparred countless rounds over the years and the 27-year-old, whose record is 15 wins with two defeats, feels he is a level above his fellow southpaw.

"It's risky to take the fight being number one with the IBF but I couldn't turn down the opportunity to fight in front of 80,000 Irish fans," Donovan said at Thursday's news conference.

"We want to bring big shows back to Ireland when Katie's gone and I'm going to be the guy to do it.

"I'm not underestimating you [McKenna], I've a job to do so I'll beat you and move onto becoming a world champion, but you're first and I'll deal with you good and proper."

'You couldn't make Taylor's story up' - Hearn

Taylor prepared for test rather than testimonial

'Dear Katie, how far we have come...' - Taylor gets reply from her hero

Veteran McKenna [25-6-1] has lost two of his last four fights after reversing a decision to retire following his own defeat by Crocker in 2023.

However, the Belfast man is not content to play the role of gatekeeper and set up camp in Philadelphia - where he spent an early part of his career - to work in 'The Dungeon' gym of Derrick 'Bozy' Ennis - father of undefeated two-division champion Jaron 'Boots'.

"To bring a west Belfast man to north Philly is a dangerous combination," said the 36-year-old.

"This is the most I've sparred in a camp, in a world-class gym surrounded by world champions and world-class fighters. The coaching has been world-class, so I've done everything for this fight.

"I think Paddy is overlooking me as all I hear is 'Liam Paro, Lewis Crocker', but you [Donovan] have to get your mind right because I'm coming for you."

Chief support on Saturday is a heavyweight contest between Dave Allen [27-9-2] and Thomas Carty [11-1].

Doncaster's Allen admits his ambitions of fighting for top honours are over following May's defeat by newly-crowned IBF heavyweight champion Filip Hrgovic.

However, he has bounced back with a pair of routine wins and feels he remains a "proper handful" at his level.

"After the Hrgovic fight, all of the feeling for boxing left me," the 34-year-old revealed.

"I'm not trying to resurrect any run for titles, I'm just here to fight but if you're not very good, I'll flatten you."

Carty once had aspirations to play Gaelic football for Dublin at Croke Park, but on Saturday he will realise something of a dream when boxing at the home of the Gaelic Athletic Association.

His sole defeat came at Madison Square Garden in March 2025 when suffering an ACL injury against Dajuan Calloway, but the 30-year-old southpaw feels he is "probably better now than what I was before" the injury.

Another Dubliner, Emmet Brennan, will make the 500-metre journey from his house to Croke Park to face fellow unbeaten super-middleweight Taylor Bevan with added incentive of double pay by Brian Peters, who represents Bevan, should he prevail.

Meanwhile, MMA convert Molly McCann continues her boxing journey against Sylwia Doligala.

McCann, who has won all four of her bouts since making the switch to professional boxing, is a relative of headliner Katie Taylor with her late grandmother a great-aunt of the Bray woman - and she recounted her own early struggles to find acceptance in the boxing world.

"I remember walking into a boxing gym and was turned away as I was a girl," said the 36-year-old Liverpudlian.

"[I] then started boxing at the Golden Gloves gym and my coach brought in a camcorder, told me to watch this girl and lo and behold, it was Katie.

"I was like 'oh my God, I want to be like that', and 20 years later here we are. It's not lost on me how many girls would kill to be in this position, so it's an honour and privilege."

title: Bradford beat Castleford to end seven-match losing run
description: Bradford Bulls end a seven-match losing streak with victory over troubled Castleford Tigers in the struggle to avoid the Super League wooden spoon.
fullText:
Tries: Dean, Wynne, Aekins, Russell, Blake, Scurr Goals: Atkin 4

Tries: Senior, Mpapalangi 2, A Mellor Goals: Weaver 3

Bradford Bulls ended their run of seven straight defeats and deepened the gloom surrounding Castleford Tigers at Odsal Stadium.

The return of three experienced forwards gave Bradford a major boost as they dominated from the start against Castleford, who are without a head coach and have now lost six of their past seven games since beating league leaders Leeds Rhinos in July.

Bottom-of-the-table Bradford took control by half-time with tries from Riley Dean, Connor Wynne, Caleb Aekins, Dan Russell and Waqa Blake as scrum-half Chris Atkin ran the show, while Louis Senior's try was Castleford's only score of the first half.

They improved in the second half with two tries from Krystian Mapapalangi and one from Alex Mellor, but Ebon Scurr's try 12 minutes after the interval was enough to keep Castleford at arm's length and move the Bulls level on points with York Knights, Huddersfield Giants and Hull FC with one game to play.

Bradford are intent on avoiding the wooden spoon in their first season back in Super League and they have given themselves a chance, especially as they face second-bottom York Knights in the final game next Thursday.

They were still a player short of naming a 21-man squad but the return of Ryan Sutton, Dan Russell and Phoenix Steinwede added punch to the pack, while Atkin was out to prove a point against his former club.

Joe Mellor sent Dean over for an early opener and Castleford were in defensive disarray as Wynne benefited from Atkin's floated pass before Aekins hacked a loose ball forward and won the race to touch it down under the posts.

Mapapalangi was a bright spot for Castleford and he sent Senior over for a try, but the ubiquitous Atkin set up both Russell and Blake for tries to end the contest by half-time.

Castleford managed to get on the front foot after the break and Mapapalangi, now over his shoulder injury, introduced an element of doubt with an early try.

Scurr was central to Bradford's forward dominance and he was rewarded with his first Super League try before Castleford's Alex Mellor forced his way over at the other end. Mapapalangi scored his second a minute before the final hooter to add some respectability to the scoreline.

Bradford coach Kurt Haggerty told BBC Radio Leeds:

"I'm really pleased with how we defended. We conceded a couple of tries off kicks which in this weather is probably the only way you are going to break teams down, but we showed resilience defensively and still managed to score some pretty special tries.

"We thought we should have got the game won over in Toulouse, so we carried the momentum over and kept our week really positive leading into this game.

"Riley [Dean] and Chris Atkin have played some games back-to-back together now and it showed. Riley was really good tonight and Chris got us around the field, a lot came through those two, but you have to give credit to our back field who carried the ball really strongly."

Castleford interim coach Luke Robinson told BBC Radio Leeds:

"We're a side that's severely lacking confidence. If we don't start well, then all of a sudden everything seems to fall apart and we don't seem to be able to have the resilience to stay in it.

"We made 30 tackles more than them before the 20-minute mark, so all you are doing is depleting yourself of energy and giving the other side a leg-up.

"The analysts told me after the game that we average 34 points a game conceded, which is a crazy stat that shows where we need to be at. The best sides are the ones that defend, and we've got to find that."

title: Kretinsky agrees to become largest West Ham shareholder
description: Czech businessman Daniel Kretinsky strikes deal to become West Ham's largest shareholder, in a move that shuts out Amanda Staveley.
fullText:
Royal Mail owner Daniel Kretinsky is to take a 46% stake in West Ham as part of a deal which will make him the club's largest shareholder.

The Czech businessman has struck a deal with the Hammers' remaining shareholders, including former chairman David Sullivan, over the 25% of the club owned by the Gold family.

The deal is likely to end former Newcastle director Amanda Staveley's immediate hopes of investing in the Championship club.

The move means Sullivan will increase his stake in the club, even though he resigned as chairman in June. He said he intended to fight allegations made against him in a joint BBC Panorama and Times investigation.

Co-chair Vanessa Gold previously agreed to sell a portion of her shares to Kretinsky in the wake of the allegations against Sullivan being made public.

However, earlier this summer, she announced an agreement to sell her entire stake to Staveley.

That triggered a complicated pre-emption rights agreement at West Ham, which gave existing directors first refusal on any significant share sale.

It is understood a deal was triggered before the deadline, resulting in Kretinsky agreeing to buy a significant portion of shares from Sullivan that will take his stake to 46% - with Sullivan's eventually rising from his current 38.8% to 40%.

A third major shareholder, Tripp Smith, will increase his ownership to 11%, with the remaining shareholders holding 3%.

The deal effectively excludes Staveley from the process.

Sullivan's status at West Ham is already being looked at by the independent regulator, although it is understood this latest move will not trigger further examination.

"The IFR's enquiries into the suitability of David Sullivan under our ODSE [owners, directors and senior executives] regime are active and ongoing and we are in touch with relevant authorities as part of this process."

Neither Kretinsky, Gold, Sullivan nor West Ham have commented on the situation.

title: No Britons left in US Open singles as Dart & Jones lose
description: Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones fall to seeded players as British interest in the US Open singles ends in the second round.
fullText:
Harriet Dart and Francesca Jones both fell to seeded players as British interest in the US Open singles ended in the second round.

Dart said she felt "under the weather" during her 6-2 6-2 defeat by Czech 25th seed Marie Bouzkova as temperatures reached around 30C in New York.

Her loss meant Jones was the last Briton standing in either singles draw, and she acquitted herself well before falling 6-4 6-4 to 14th seed and rising American star Iva Jovic.

Nine British players competed in the US Open main draws - the most since 1981 - with four coming through qualifying.

Five of them reached the second round, but Jacob Fearnley was the only player to win a set as they all fell to seeded players.

Lucky loser Fearnley fell in four sets to 27th seed Tomas Martin Etcheverry, while qualifier Toby Samuel was beaten by 18th seed Jiri Lehecka.

Katie Boulter lost to Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova in only 58 minutes on Wednesday.

In the men's draw, Cameron Norrie, Arthur Fery, Harry Wendelken and Jan Choinski exited in the first round.

Jones, ranked 90 places lower than Jovic, made the American work for one hour and 54 minutes to reach the third round.

Humid conditions meant both players frequently dashed to the back of the court between points to dry their hands and face.

It was Jovic who started on the front foot, opening up a double break and a 3-0 lead as the 18-year-old controlled the rallies with some deep hitting from the baseline.

Jones snatched a break back and kept in touch with Jovic - but she could not make the most of a break point as Jovic served for the set.

After wrapping up the opener, Jovic raced into a 4-1 lead in the second, only to once again be dragged back by Jones.

The Briton saved three match points on her own serve but Jovic produced one of her best service games to seal victory and set up a meeting with good friend Alexandra Eala.

Dart, who is ranked 131st in the world, struggled on serve against Bouzkova, committing eight double faults and landing only 45% of her first serves.

Dart draped ice towels around her neck and used cold-air hoses at the changeovers against Bouzkova as she attempted to cool down.

"I have been a bit under the weather. It is what it is, sadly," Dart, 30, said.

"It was quite warm. I had a temperature, I was trying to cool down. I've played many weeks in a row.

"I am not used to air conditioning being pumped everywhere. We go from really hot outside to freezing inside.

"All credit to my opponent, she is an incredibly tough player, so even if I had been at full capacity, I don't know."

Bouzkova took command almost straight away, winning seven games in a row to clinch the first set and go a double break up in the second.

From there Dart was unable to recover as Bouzkova safely saw out the rest of the match to reach the third round, where she will face Polish eighth seed Iga Swiatek.

title: Obano to put England career on hold with Pau move

fullText:
Beno Obano will become the latest England player to put his Test career on ice with a move to France, after agreeing to join Top 14 side Pau from Bath at the end of the forthcoming season.

The 31-year-old loose-head prop won his fifth cap in the defeat by South Africa in July, backing up first-choice Ellis Genge off the bench.

Head coach Steve Borthwick is restricted to a domestic-based talent pool as a key part of the relationship between Prem clubs and the Rugby Football Union over elite players.

England are relatively well stocked at loose-head, with Harlequins' Fin Baxter, Northampton's Emmanuel Iyogun and Sale's Bevan Rodd all younger than Obano and vying for a role.

Sale's versatile 22-year-old Asher Opoku-Fordjour can also pack down on that side of the front row.

It is unlikely England will rule out selecting Obano this season, as they did when Tom Willis announced in October that he would move to Bordeaux-Begles for 2026-27.

Despite starting three matches in the 2025 Six Nations, impressing in a summer series win over Argentina and being awarded a central contract for the year, Willis was exiled from the squad, with Borthwick instead focusing on players who would be available for the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Obano, who isn't on a central contract, will be available for the tournament, just as David Ribbans and Joe Marchant were when they went into the 2023 edition having agreed moves to France for the following season.

He will join an impressive list of England talent out in France with Jack Willis, Kyle Sinckler, Billy Vunipola, Manu Tuilagi, Lewis Ludlam and Sam Simmonds all currently playing their club rugby across the Channel and outside England eligibility.

Obano's departure will cause Bath more front-row upheaval. South African powerhouse Thomas du Toit left for the Durban-based Sharks at the end of the last campaign, while Scotland international Jamie Bhatti arrived this summer.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan says he is "really keen" to host the proposed Tyson Fury-Anthony Joshua fight at Wembley Stadium and has urged promoters to get in touch.

BBC Sport understands Saudi organisers Sela have contacted the mayor's office in recent weeks about bringing the long-awaited contest to the national stadium.

However, with organisers and broadcaster Netflix understood to favour New York's Madison Square Garden for a November bout, sources close to the discussions say talks over a London venue have not progressed, with no detailed talks over dates or timings.

"A message to the promoters - we want to host it in London. Talk to us, we're really keen to have it," Khan told BBC Sport on Thursday.

Wembley Stadium's usual curfew is 23:00, although Khan has previously indicated he would support efforts to bring the fight to London.

A late-night fight in London - potentially in the early hours - could mean it draws a larger television audience in the US.

Brent Council, the local authority involved in any approval, has said a potential extension of the curfew would need to be assessed by Wembley's safety advisory group.

It remains unclear how late that curfew could be pushed back.

"Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury are two great British boxers. Both have been world champions," Khan said.

"They both recognise and love the fans in this country who have supported them throughout their careers, amateur and professional.

"Wembley has hosted many fantastic events, including bouts involving Tyson and Anthony. We, the fans, want to see them box live in London."

There is hope that the venue will be finalised in the coming days. Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn has said he wants an announcement this week, with a news conference to follow next week.

BBC Sport has contacted Sela for comment.

Fury calls Joshua a 'coward' as wait for announcement continues

Hearn says his side signed a contract for the bout to take place in the United Kingdom, while Sela and Netflix's preference would be the United States, to cater for American audiences.

Matchroom Boxing's Hearn has previously said Joshua's contract specifically stipulated a UK venue and would need to be renegotiated for the fight to take place Stateside.

Hearn says he has since set out terms under which Matchroom would agree to the change, with negotiations continuing over a possible move to New York.

The contact from Sela represents a significant development from the end of July, when sources close to the mayor told BBC Sport there had been no approach from the fight's organisers.

But the lack of progress since that initial contact underlines the uncertainty still surrounding Wembley's chances of hosting the contest.

"I'm hoping the promoters understand that not only will you get 100,000 people watching this bout live, you'll get millions watching it across the globe, where both boxers are cheered on by their loyal fans," Khan said.

title: Kyrgios given one-month ban for positive cocaine test
description: Nick Kyrgios is eligible to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive for cocaine.
fullText:
Nick Kyrgios is eligible to return to tennis after accepting a one-month ban for testing positive for cocaine.

The Australian, 31, was provisionally suspended on 4 August after a sample he submitted during the Mallorca Open in June was found to contain benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine.

Kyrgios told investigators from the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) that he used cocaine at a nightclub in Magaluf in the early hours of 20 June.

He played his first-round match at the Mallorca tournament two days later, losing in straight sets to compatriot Adam Walton.

The ITIA accepted he used cocaine outside of competition after consulting with an an independent expert.

Kyrgios could have faced a maximum three-month ban but it has been reduced to one month after he entered a treatment programme.

His one-month ban ended on Thursday, 3 September.

Kyrgios, who has fallen to 918 in the world rankings, will also lose his prize money of 6,570 euros (£5,650).

When the positive test was announced, Kyrgios said he would step away from social media and public life for the next 28 days to "focus on getting myself right".

The former world number 13 has played just four singles matches this season, having struggled with knee and wrist injuries in recent years.

He last played in the men's doubles at Wimbledon, where he and partner Alexander Bublik lost in the first round.

After his initial suspension was announced, Kyrgios said the past few years of injuries had taken "a huge toll on me, both mentally and physically".

"My body hasn't been able to do what my mind expects it to do," he wrote in a lengthy statement on Instagram.

"Coming to terms with being near the end of my career has been harder than I ever imagined.

"None of that excuses what I did."

Cocaine is classified as a stimulant and substance of abuse on the World Anti-Doping Agency's prohibited list.

Kyrgios has long been a controversial figure in tennis.

His behaviour on court has been widely criticised and he has been given numerous large fines for smashing racquets, making audible obscenities and arguing with the umpire.

In 2023, he admitted assaulting an ex-girlfriend two years earlier. He avoided a criminal conviction.

He was criticised further for making a series of comments which have been considered misogynistic.

In 2024 he shared a post from controversial influencer Andrew Tate. He later said he had gone "to all lengths" to distance himself from the self-proclaimed misogynist.

Kyrgios was also critical of the handling of two high-profile anti-doping cases involving top players Jannik Sinner and Iga Swiatek, calling them "disgusting" for tennis.

Kyrgios has won seven ATP Tour singles titles and reached the Wimbledon final in 2022, losing in four sets to Novak Djokovic.

He and compatriot Thanasi Kokkinakis won the Australian Open men's doubles title together in 2022.

Kyrgios has also spoken about his struggles with mental health, saying he "genuinely contemplated" suicide and spent time in a psychiatric hospital in London after losing at Wimbledon in 2019.

Kyrgios took cocaine at a nightclub in Magaluf two days before his match, and less than 24 hours before he would have been considered 'in competition.'

That is because the singles draw began on 21 June, even though Kyrgios did not play his first-round match until the following day.

The ban is only one month as Kyrgios has provided an invoice which shows he has paid for a treatment programme, which began on 28 August.

The Australian has thus been banned for the same amount of time as Iga Swiatek - and two months fewer than Jannik Sinner.

Kyrgios felt both of those bans were overly lenient and has previously described the tennis integrity system as "awful."

He is free to play again with immediate effect, but has found it very difficult to get on court since reaching the 2022 Wimbledon final.

Kyrgios has had knee and reconstructive wrist surgery and won only two of the eight matches he has been able to play since the start of 2023.

fullText:
Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world

Kat Jones may be the closest thing Scotland has to Erin Brockovich in 2026. Standing in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat outside Holyrood, the 52-year-old is revving up the crowd of protesters around her. “Who is here from Lammermuir? Ayrshire? What about Aberdeen?” she calls to the crowd.

On Thursday, hundreds travelled to Edinburgh to call for an immediate moratorium on Scotland’s datacentre boom, which includes one project in Auchtertool, Fife, that has been billed as the second largest in the world.

Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, is spearheading a campaign demanding a pause while the Scottish government produces analysis on the environmental impact of the centres, and clear planning guidance on the definition of a “green” datacentre.

She is a whirr of action: greeting, encouraging, emailing and introducing. Thursday’s protest was the biggest yet.

In John Swinney’s programme for government on Tuesday, Scotland’s equivalent to the king’s speech, the first minister said he would take a strategic approach to datacentres with “expectations around environmental sustainability, resource use, community benefit”, but stopped short of agreeing to a moratorium.

For the campaigners, this is not enough. From Dubar to Greenock, there is fierce anger at the speed and scale of the projects in the planning pipeline. At least 20 are proposed so far, with more rumoured. Some are planned in the countryside not far from small villages, others next to care homes and residential housing.

Kathleen White, who is campaigning against a proposed £2bn datacentre in Lammermuir hills in the Scottish borders, said the project did not make any sense in her area.

“We are from a small village of about a hundred people. The project is planned about a mile up the road,” she said.

“There’s a reservoir and an angling spot. It’s an upland area with dark skies. The datacentre buildings would cover eight hectares [20 acres] of mostly concrete in a greenfield area. It is going to be a monstrosity.”

The rising public anger about the datacentre buildout that underpins the global AI boom is a growing threat to the UK’s strategy. Keir Starmer’s government leaned heavily on AI as a means to turbocharge a limp economy while he was prime minister.

Crucial to this were “AI growth zones”, which were areas where Britain planned to build massive AI datacentres in the hope that jobs and growth would follow. The Guardian’s investigations have called into question the numbers and reasoning behind this strategy.

The UK’s grid is strained, and proposed datacentres are meeting stiff resistance in London and elsewhere in the south of England.

This spring, British officials pushed would-be AI datacentre developers to look north – suggesting Scotland, with its renewable energy and abundant water resources, is better-equipped to support the country’s efforts to keep up in the AI race. One of the UK’s five AI growth zones will be in Lanarkshire, a rural area outside Glasgow.

Mounting public anger – and a potential moratorium – could jeopardise this pivot. But Jones rejects any suggestion that the moratorium campaign is standing in the way of progress.

“People who are campaigning locally on issues that matter to them a lot get accused of being nimbys. But this is a campaign that has national and international consequences. Datacentres are some of the biggest buildings on the planet, they use so much energy.

“Local campaigners are the most motivated to oppose them because they are a direct existential threat to the places they love, right near their homes, near hospitals, near schools.”

The opposition to large-scale datacentres has also been backed by the Scottish Greens and by Reform UK. Reform has raised concerns about the number of projects, while the Scottish Greens have backed the moratorium – echoing the campaigners’ demands for a national framework.

Ross Greer, co-leader of the Scottish Greens, who was outside Holyrood with protesters, said: “If we want to have the internet, we need datacentres and Scotland already has plenty of them.

“But some of these new hyper-scale datacentres of 120MW to 200MW – in total, those proposed would require more energy than all of Scotland needs at its peak at the moment. That is clearly not possible.”

The Scottish government has said that all planning authorities must notify ministers of new datacentre applications exceeding 50MW within a week to help monitor their impact on infrastructure, but underscored that the centres are important for economic growth.

The public finance minister for Scotland, Hannah Mary Goodlad, said: “We must balance the economic and employment interests in developing datacentres with national energy, climate and community wealth building ambitions, which are vital to our future prosperity, as well as the potential impact on local communities.

“I am clear that voices of communities that will be affected will be central to any considerations on datacentres.”

But Jones and the campaign want more. She fears that Scotland could be overwhelmed without a formal national strategy. “We are not saying everything needs to stop for ever. But it’s moving so fast. We need a pause.”

fullText:
Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’

The president of OpenAI, Greg Brockman, has claimed the world has entered a new era of artificial general intelligence after the release of his company’s latest model, Astra, which it described as the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model”.

Brockman made the claim on Thursday as the San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern and a pause in Astra’s training.

Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI has defined it as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”.

Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.

“I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.”

OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours.

Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.”

Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”.

Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training. They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts.

Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”.

But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences.

On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol. On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources.

But OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said: “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.”

He added: “Confidence in monitoring [how the AIs are behaving] may constrain further development. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.”

The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals.

The race to release ever-more advanced AIs comes as OpenAI pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). Anthropic is also targeting an IPO which could value it as high as $2tn.

Meanwhile, more than 1,000 employees at frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently signed a joint letter this summer that warned the companies were “under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration”. They called on the US government to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”
